SR² Hand documentation · index of result pages · topic overview: printed fingertips and force sensing · updated 2026-10-27

Finite elements, magnetic readout and contact estimation of the printed TPU fingertips

The printed fingertip has five magnets in a soft thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) pad and five magnetic sensors behind it. A press deforms the pad, moves the magnets and changes the sensors’ readings. We model that sequence to estimate where the tool presses and with how much force. On a UR5 arm, with a six-axis force sensor as the reference, the untrained model placed presses of 2 N and more within 0.9–2.4 mm. Its force was 0.78–1.31 of the reference. Below 1.5 N it placed presses 8–10 mm off with the first tips’ weak magnets, and within 2.0 mm with five N52 magnets. Trained on a tip’s own presses, a Gaussian process placed presses at new points within 0.25–0.53 mm at 1.5 N and over. It gave the force’s direction within 2.1–2.5° on the face. A model learned on one tip misses on another by 1.4–2.5 mm, and by 0.64 mm once each board change is scaled by its magnets’ strength. A neighbouring fingertip’s magnets change a board by up to 4,162 µT, against 23 µT for a 0.5 N press. Under a small sphere the printed pad sinks further than its finite-element model predicts. Three pages explain this in order: the physical model of the pad and its readout, the calibration on the UR5, and the first part of the contact overview, which compares the print with the simulations’ sphere pads.

One press through the model

At rest, the five chips measure the field from the magnets inside the pad. Each chip measures the field in three directions, giving 15 numbers. A press moves the magnets by a few micrometres and changes those numbers. The change depends on both the contact point and the force, so one chip alone cannot generally separate them.

Finite-element analysis divides the printed walls, solid skins and gyroid infill into small pieces. It predicts how a force at each candidate point moves the magnets. A magnetic-field model then predicts the 15 readings. For a live press, the estimator searches for the point and force whose predicted change fits the measured one. The print model, board readout, estimator and UR5 presses give the calculations and measurements.

Terms

Approach
Travel of a rigid indenter into the tip from first touch under a given normal force, in µm; the reference indenter is the 12.5 mm screwdriver shaft across the finger.
Wall, skin, core
The three printed structures. Walls are the two 0.45 mm perimeters of every layer (0.9 mm), also around each magnet pocket. Skins are the four solid 0.2 mm layers under every top and bottom surface (0.8 mm). The core is the gyroid infill.
Infill setting, solid fraction
The slicer’s gyroid density setting (30 or 50 %) and the volume fraction of TPU it prints, which differ because successive layers’ beads overlap only in part.
Homogenized tensor
The 6×6 elasticity tensor of a periodic cell of printed gyroid, per unit modulus of solid TPU : the stiffness of the core seen at the scale of the tip.
Contact modulus
The modulus of the sphere pads’ pressure law that best reproduces the FE approach at 0.5, 1 and 3 N, in MPa; the RL scenes use 10 MPa.
Magnet travel
Rigid motion of a magnet per newton of contact force, from the FE, in µm/N.
Sensing plane
The plane of the five chips’ Hall elements; on concept b it lies 0.42 mm below the pad’s back face.
Force resolution
The Cramér–Rao bound on the standard deviation of the pressing force, in N. It is computed from one conversion of the five chips (141 Hz) at a known contact point, with Earth’s field unknown. It is the spread of the best unbiased estimate when the models are exact.
Sphere pads
The simulations’ contact model of the tip: 0.75 mm spheres on a 1 mm lattice over its surface. Each has stiffness , with its depth below the tip’s volume centroid (builder v2).
Rest calibration
The fit of the field model to the reading with the pad untouched. It gives which chip address sits at which position, the chips’ axes, every magnet’s pole, the magnets’ strength and the pad’s offset on the board.
Sensitivity
The change of the 15 readings per newton of a patch load at surface point , along each axis of the tip frame (15×3).
Placed away
A simulated press whose estimated point lies more than 1.5 mm from the true one.
HEX-E
The OptoForce HEX-E six-axis force-torque sensor between the UR5’s flange and the calibration mount: the force reference of the UR5 sessions.
Touch-off, registration
A slow approach of the pad onto an indenter until the push begins. The registration fits the tool’s pose and the indenter’s centre to many touch-offs.
Hold
One force level of a press on the UR5, kept for about 1.5 s: one sample of the ground truth and of the board.
Location error
The distance in mm from an estimated contact point to the true one, tangential to the pad; a median over holds.
Physical model
The estimator of this page on a pad’s rest calibration, with no training.
Tip frame
along the pad’s normal toward the palmar face, across the finger, from the mount toward the tip end, in mm.

Components of the fingertip and its models

The fingertip is concept b of the DIP-link study, which the owner chose after the first prints of 2026-10-20. The pad is the front 13.45 of the 17.0 mm of the 11/22 half-ellipsoid tip of the simulations. It slides into a PLA cover on the DIP link, over the ReSkin 5X board. The board’s chips lie 0.42 mm below the pad’s back face; the current link is b v4 (DIP link b v4). Five N52 magnets, a centre one and four corners 7.4 mm apart, sit with their tops 7.5 mm under the apex. That is the shallowest depth that keeps 1.8 mm of TPU around every pocket. A press moves the magnets by a few micrometres; the chips read the change of their field.

Each box is one model with its own check. The finite elements resolve what the printer makes: walls, skins and gyroid. The walls take the load at the face’s edges, and so they set the patch that the pads must reproduce. The field model represents each magnet as a cylinder of 72 dipoles, because a single dipole is 5.5 % high at the chips’ distance. The rest calibration makes the chain usable on a pad as built. From 2 s of untouched reading it finds the chips’ layout and the magnets’ poles and strength. Forward, the chain ranks designs by their force resolution before anything is printed. Inverted, it turns readings into a contact point and a force without a robot.

The printed pad

The pads print in Siraya Tech 85A on the Prusa XL’s tool 2 or the P1S’s external spool. The nozzle is at 240 °C and the bed at 35 °C. The pad prints upright in 0.1 mm layers, with two perimeters outside and around each pocket, four top and four bottom layers, and gyroid at 30 or 50 %. The print pauses at 9.2 and 16.2 mm of height so that the magnets can be placed, north toward the palmar face. Each magnet sits in a pocket with a 2.9 mm seat and is held by press fit (the owner’s choice from the seat coupon, 2026-10-18). The recipe stays the same on every printer, so one FE describes every pad (print procedure). The pads weigh 0.6 % more TPU than the FE assumes, and concept a’s tips 3.0 % less, about 7 % softer (DIP link b v3 and mount v2).

85A at 30 % gyroid was chosen for the magnets’ travel: the softer the pad, the more field change per newton, until the approach outgrows what 1 mm pads represent. The rule from the co-design study is at least 12 µm/N of travel for 0.1 N (fingertip co-design); the 95A tips of the first studies gave 11.7 µm/N at best. eFlesh lattices, printed open as eFlesh prints them, give 250 µm/N of travel, but they sink 613 µm at 1 N and print with unsupported islands. With a skin closing every face they sink 81 µm and give 0.075 N, which is the gyroid’s resolution (eFlesh printability).

Finite elements of the printed structure

Materials. The tip’s shape is voxelized at 0.05 mm. In each layer plane, TPU within 0.9 mm of the outline is wall. TPU within 0.8 mm of an exposed surface along the build axis is skin. The rest is core. The magnets are a fourth class, and walls and skins line their pockets as the slicer prints them. The classes are sampled onto a graded hexahedral grid, 0.2–0.25 mm under the face and 0.8–1.1 mm deep inside (about 120–220 thousand degrees of freedom). Walls and skins are solid TPU, isotropic with Poisson 0.45. Their modulus is 30 MPa for 95A and 12 MPa for 85A, from datasheets; NinjaFlex stands in for Siraya’s unmeasured 85A. The magnets are NdFeB at 160 GPa, bonded (finite elements of the printed tip).

Gyroid core. The core is homogenized from the gyroid as the slicer prints it. In each 0.2 mm layer the toolpath follows the zero set of the gyroid function at mid-layer, with a 0.45 mm bead. Successive layers bond only where their beads overlap:

A periodic cell of these voxels takes six unit macroscopic strains ; each load case solves for the periodic fluctuation , and the effective tensor is the cell’s mean stress:

The result is orthotropic, and it is stiffer along the build axis. At the settings used, 30 % prints 32.6 % solid. Its modulus is in the layer plane and along the build axis. The setting 50 % prints 55.0 % solid, with 0.228 and 0.311. Over 11–42 % solid the moduli follow and in the solid fraction . These fits lie between the bending and stretching limits of Gibson and Ashby.

Tip model and contact. The elements are eight-node hexahedra with Wilson–Taylor incompatible modes, so the thin walls bend without shear locking. A 40-voxel cantilever comes out 2.4 % below beam theory, against 9.8 % for plain hexahedra. Each element takes the tensor of its class, and the core’s tensor is rotated into the tip frame. Concept b’s pad is fixed at its cut face and the mount face. One sparse Cholesky factorization of is reused for every load. A rigid frictionless indenter (the shaft, a plate or a sphere) meets the face nodes. Their normal compliance comes from columns of . At approach the nodal forces solve

and is bisected until equals the load. A magnet’s motion is the rigid fit of its nodes’ displacements. Each gap is measured from the tip’s analytic surface; on the curved tips the grid’s face nodes lie a median 0.10–0.13 mm from that surface (95th percentile 0.43–0.49 mm).

Solver. The solver is our own Python (scripts/tpu_tip_fem_core.py; SciPy, CHOLMOD and PyAMG on the CPU, PyTorch on the GPU). Its input is voxels: the slicer’s material classes at 0.05 mm, or every gyroid bead at 0.1 mm. On a voxel grid all elements of one size share one element matrix. The model resolving every bead, 1.7–2.2 million elements and 5–8 million degrees of freedom, is then solved matrix-free on the GPU in 2–3 GB and 60–140 s per approach. The off-the-shelf solvers installed for the study run on the CPU from tetrahedral meshes. FEniCSx took 3.3–5.7 GB for 0.45–0.68 million degrees of freedom of quadratic tetrahedra. At that rate the resolved tip needs above 40 GB, and the workstation has 30 GB. PolyFEM’s IPC contact took 7–14 min for 57 thousand degrees of freedom. One element code solves the periodic cells, the homogenized tip and the resolved tip, so their comparison tests the homogenization alone. FEniCSx and PolyFEM remain as checks (finite elements of the printed tip, Tables 7 and 8).

Checks. On the 95A block of the first study the model is 1.9 % off Hertz under a 40 mm sphere. With every bead resolved at 0.1 mm, the approach is within 2.6 % of the homogenized tip’s (44.8 against 46.0 µm at 1 N). The same check was run on the 85A 11/22 tip and b’s pad, with 6–8 million degrees of freedom on the GPU. It puts the resolved beads 1.6–4.8 % stiffer than the homogenized core under the rods, and up to 7.8 % stiffer under a 2 mm sphere. About 1 % of that comes from the cell’s voxel size. A finer contact grid changes the approach by at most 3.6 % (v2 fingertip checks, Section 6; calibration to the finite elements). Pad B00 was solved from its G-code. Under the rod at 1 N it sinks 18 % less than the design pad when its beads are drawn at their nominal widths. Those widths put 11 % more TPU in the model than the printed parts weigh. With its TPU set to the weighed volume the pad sinks 3.9 % less. Its 0.1 mm layers make the gyroid 8 % stiffer in the layer plane. With that cell the homogenized pad agrees with the G-code model within 1 % under the rod (v2 fingertip checks). The G-code solve of the 95A tip of 10-13 read none of the G-code’s arc moves, which are 11 % of its filament. With them the tip sinks 33 µm at 1 N against the design model’s 41, where the earlier reading gave 63 (eFlesh printability).

Effects of the design changes

Each change below was solved on the same models. Approaches are under the 12.5 mm shaft at 1 N, and resolutions are per sample at the contact point (finite elements of the printed tip, v2 fingertip checks).

Two choices follow from the table. Five magnets are used, because the centre magnet over U1 halves the resolution of four. Concept b is used, because the cut pad puts the magnets 3.5 mm closer to the chips. The cover walls and the cap cost at most 16 % of the resolution, in the bound that fixes the flanks both ways.

Magnetic readout and force resolution

The ReSkin 5X board has five MLX90393 three-axis Hall magnetometers in a plus, U1 at the centre and U2–U5 7.00 mm from it. Each chip senses 0.42 mm under its package top. The chips are read over the STEMMA QT port of a QT Py ESP32-S3 in 2.0 ms, 375 records a second. Each chip converts every 7.0–7.1 ms (140–143 Hz). The firmware sets the gain at GAIN_SEL 1, RES 1. That gives 1.20 µT a count on and , 1.94 on , and a range of 38.4 mT. This gain is used because b’s five magnets put 27.5 mT on the nearest chip, and the most sensitive gain covers only 4.8 mT. At rest the measured noise per sample is 1.54–1.76 µT on and and 2.32–2.59 µT on , 1.4 times the datasheet model for this gain. Three fingers’ boards answer at the same addresses and need an I²C multiplexer. Three fingers on one multiplexer were read together on 2026-10-25 at 152 records a second, so every conversion of the 15 chips is read. Each chip’s noise matched that of the same finger read alone to within 2 %, and the boards’ readings did not correlate (at most 0.031) (magnetometer readout, src/morphohand/driver/reskin5x/README.md). Three v1 fingertips left at rest on one multiplexer for 8.4 h on 2026-10-26/27 were read without a gap, and the viewer showed no contact at its 2 µT floor (three fingertips at rest).

The design studies rank layouts by force resolution. The FE gives each magnet’s translation and rotation per newton of a patch load. The field model turns that into the change of the 15 readings, which is the sensitivity . The noise then bounds how well a force can be read. With a uniform background field (Earth’s) unknown, and the contact point too when it is unknown,

the Cramér–Rao bound on the pressing force from one sample. It is a lower bound: it assumes the models are exact. On the first 95A tip one 4.76 mm magnet 5 mm deep resolved 0.044 N at a known point. When the point was unknown it resolved 0.08–1.48 N over the face. For that reason the layouts went to four magnets (0.14 N everywhere) and then five. On the 11/22 tip concept a resolves 0.065 N and b resolves 0.028 N. The contact is located to 0.34 × 0.42 mm with b and 1.40 × 1.31 mm with a. At the measured noise b’s 0.028 N becomes about 0.039 N (v2 fingertip checks).

The disturbances are larger than the noise. The chips run without their on-chip temperature compensation. Each chip’s sensitivity falls by 0.65–0.70 % per °C of its die temperature. On the centre chip, in 7.6 mT, one degree is 53 µT, which is twice a 1 N press on the face. The board warms by about 1 °C in the minutes after it is plugged in. Dividing each reading by its chip’s gain at the chip’s own temperature leaves 9 of those 70 µT (contact estimation, Section 9). On the first tip, a facing fingertip’s magnet moving from 25 to 30 mm read as 5.16 N, and as 2.01 N with the field’s gradient estimated. The other magnets’ positions follow from the hand’s joint angles, so their field can be subtracted. Earth’s field, 1.71 N on U1 alone, drops out of the five-chip estimate. The board must not move against the pad. On concept a with four magnets, 1 µm of board motion reads as 0.160 N, and for that reason the board is clamped (DIP link board mount).

Contact point and force from the readings

The estimator runs the chain backwards (contact estimation). At rest the 15 components are the magnets’ field and Earth’s. The rotation of each chip is taken from the board’s pick-and-place file, and one common offset is fitted. The rest calibration then finds which address sits at which position. It also finds every magnet’s pole, the magnets’ strength and the pad’s offset on the board. On pad B00 as first assembled it fits at 0.43 mT RMS against fields of 1.9–7.0 mT. It finds magnets at 35 % of an N52’s moment, with two diagonal corners reversed. The owner confirmed that these magnets were not N52 and went in at random. A press then changes the reading by

where comes from an FE basis of 1 N loads along , and at the 812 pad points. The points cover the whole free surface (2,436 load cases, 101 s, 2.0 GB). A thin-plate spline interpolates between the points. The vector contains a uniform field change and a strength change, each with a Gaussian prior. With the covariance of the noise and the nuisance terms and a force prior  N, the force at each candidate point and the point itself follow from

the log marginal likelihood of a contact at . It is maximized over 12,581 candidate points about 0.2 mm apart, with the force pressing, inside a friction cone of 2 and below 25 N. The determinant charges each point for the patterns it could explain. Without it the best fit often went to a flank point where the reading barely responds, with forces of 100 N and more. The Fisher information gives each estimate’s 1-sigma; one estimate takes 1.2 ms.

Of 600 simulated presses with N52 magnets and the 50 ms window, 2 % are placed more than 1.5 mm away. The rest have median errors of 0.20 mm and 0.036 N on the face, and 0.17 mm and 0.050 N on the flanks. The errors follow the predicted 1-sigma (ratio 1.10–1.16). With the magnets in the pad today, 15 % are placed away and the rest have 0.39 mm and 0.08 N. Over 30 s without a press, one frame of 880 shows a contact.

Steel near the pad is magnetized by the magnets, and its field at the chips is that of the magnets’ mirror images. A 100 g mass and a steel ruler, touched to the second fingertip’s face without force, changed the reading by 217 to 360 µT. Each touch was estimated as a press of 9.0 to 17.5 N on a side wall. The images lie four times as far from the chips as the magnets, so their field varies little across the board. A uniform field and a linear gradient fit 94 to 98 % of each touch’s change and 28 to 30 % of a press’s. With the viewer’s key f, each contact is compared with such a field and not shown when the field fits better by more than 25 in chi-square (fields from outside the pad). The frames shown as contacts during six touches fell from 432 to 29. Of 20,851 contact frames in the UR5 streams, 117 were rejected, none inside a hold. A press made with a steel object is rejected where the object’s field dominates, so the test is off by default.

Calibration against the HEX-E on the UR5

The calibration presses the pad on indenters fixed in the lab’s UR5 cell, with the HEX-E between the flange and the mount (calibration protocol). The HEX-E is 35 mm tall, so the face centre lies 128.4 mm from the flange. A session homes the tool on the indenter’s key and fits the HEX-E’s offsets in a gravity sweep. Touch-offs of the pad on a sphere of radius 5 mm then register the tool and the sphere’s centre to the pad. Presses follow the surface normal at points over the face, the edges and the flanks, at force levels of 0.25 to 5 N. Rolls and twists turn the pad on the sphere. In a simulated session the registration gives the contact point within 0.07 mm and the force within 0.4 % (medians).

The program runs on the lab’s computer, which pushes each run for this workstation to analyse (lab runs). In the session sphere2 of 2026-10-22, 29 touch-offs registered the tool with a residual of 57 µm RMS on the pad. They moved the tool centre point by 2.01 mm and 2.81° from its CAD and homing values. Then 74 presses gave 357 holds, and 10 rolls and twists gave 78 more. Over 65 min the reference press kept its onset within 0.07 mm and its depth within 0.05 mm, so the pad stayed in its seat.

Under the sphere the board’s force agrees with the HEX-E’s. Its slope against the HEX-E’s normal force is 0.83 on the face, 0.78 on the edges and 1.05 on the flanks. The registered indentation is larger than the FE pad’s at the measured force: at that depth the FE pad would push back with 5.1 times the measured force. If the pad itself were that much softer than its model, the magnets would move about five times as far per newton. The board would then read about five times the HEX-E’s force. The pad’s bulk therefore lies within about 22 % of the FE model. The extra indentation fits 0.33 mm plus 0.20 mm per newton, in parts whose motion the magnets do not see (UR5 ground truth and predictors, Sections 3 and 4). Presses under a rod of radius 12.5 mm, in the sessions of 2026-10-23, travel 0.07 mm plus 0.10 mm per newton beyond the FE pad. A spring in series with the pad, in the mount, the arm or the indenter’s stand, would add the same travel per newton under both indenters. At most 0.10 mm/N therefore lies in series. At least 0.10 mm/N arises at the sphere’s contact, where the FE pad is stiffer than the print (Section 8 of the same page).

From 1 N up, the untrained estimator places contacts 1.6 to 2.6 mm from the registered points (medians by force level). Its forces are within 10 to 26 % of the HEX-E’s. At 3 N and over its mean error is a systematic offset of 1.4 mm. Under the rod its force is 0.63 of the HEX-E’s on the face and 0.71 on the edges. Below 1 N it places contacts a median 9.8 mm away. Each press leaves the rest about 7 µT off, the change of 0.3 N, and below 1 N that step is as large as the press itself.

Learned models do better on the same pad. A Gaussian process (GP) from the board change to the contact point and normal force was trained on 59 presses. It places 15 held-out presses within 0.84 mm and 0.086 N. On the same holds the untrained estimator gives 3.79 mm and 0.382 N. An ensemble of five small multilayer perceptrons (MLP) gives 0.74 mm and 0.061 N. Over four folds the MLP gives 0.79 mm and the GP 1.00 mm. On the rolls and twists, at orientations that no press had, the GP gives 2.05 mm, the MLP 2.93 mm and the untrained estimator 2.44 mm. Trained on 45 rod presses, the MLP places held-out contacts within 0.57 mm and the GP within 1.05 mm.

The learned models held a day later. The lab repeated 27 of sphere2’s grid presses about 18 h later. Trained on all of the night’s presses, the GP placed their contacts within 0.80 mm and the MLP within 0.71 mm. At 1 and 2 N the board change at the same target differed from the night’s by 38 and 20 %. The night’s own repeats of one press differed by 35 and 23 %. The pad met the sphere about 0.15 mm earlier at the same force (UR5 ground truth and predictors, Section 9).

Over the 2.3 h session the board’s zero moved by up to 71 µT. Earth’s field, turning with the tool, made 98 % of that change, and the estimator absorbs it as a uniform field. A press leaves a step of 7 µT along its own change. Of that step 0.29 lasts, and the rest fades with a time constant of 19 s. No learned zero beat a re-zero at rest before each press (board drift).

The HEX-E is a weak reference. Its Fz channel reads 0.78 and 0.87 of the other axes’ gain in two gravity fits, and its link failed in three of the first night’s eight runs. An ATI Mini45 of the lab is to replace it. It will first be calibrated on the UR5 with a weighed mass hung at five points (39 stations, about 27 min). In simulated sessions that calibration recovers the sensor to 0.021 N with the lab’s 100 g weight in a printed holder, and to 0.005 N with a 0.5 kg mass (medians) (ATI calibration plan).

Transfer to other magnets and a second fingertip

A calibration learned on one pad must also work on a pad with other magnets. This was simulated on sphere2’s mechanics: each hold keeps its true point and force, and its board change is synthesized for other magnets. The physical model, rebuilt from each set’s rest calibration, gives 2.02 mm with today’s magnets. It gives 1.52 mm with N52 magnets all one way. It gives 1.36 mm with N52 magnets in the checkerboard now printed, with the centre magnet and one diagonal one way and the other diagonal the other way. Trained on today’s magnets, a GP on the raw board change is off by 1.64 and 4.09 mm on the two N52 sets. A GP that corrects the physical estimate, with that estimate as its input, gives 0.73 and 0.83 mm. Retrained on the checkerboard, the GP gives 0.61 mm. On sphere2’s real presses the corrected estimate is off by 1.50 mm over four folds, and the MLP by 0.79 mm (UR5 ground truth and predictors, Tables 8 and 9).

The second fingertip on the workstation’s desk has its two magnets at the mount end reversed. Its rest reading alone gave that pattern, at 0.25 mT RMS against 1.06 mT for the next pattern. With the fingertip fixed to the desk, the owner pressed the face centre six times with the 5 mm sphere indenter. The physical model rebuilt from the rest fit placed the six within 0.93 mm of their mean. That mean lies 3.07 mm from the reference point, which was aimed at by eye, at 2.9 to 4.4 N. For all six presses sphere2’s GP on the raw board change returned one and the same point. Its MLP put them 9.9 mm away. Sphere2’s correction moved the points 2.3 mm toward the mount end. No force was measured, so the correction is not yet scored on this pad (second fingertip).

The first checkerboard tip was then pressed on the UR5 against the HEX-E (session cb1t, on the evening of 2026-10-23: 302 press holds and 64 turn holds). One pole pattern fits its field at rest, at 0.24 mT against 0.87 mT for the next. It is the planned checkerboard: the owner had named its poles from the board’s side. Built from that fit alone, the physical model placed held-out contacts within 2.06 mm and 0.28 N, against 3.79 mm and 0.38 N on sphere2’s tip. At 2 N and over its error was 1.1 to 1.2 mm. Trained on sphere2’s presses, no learned model came closer. The GP on the raw board change missed by 5.3 mm, and sphere2’s correction of the physical estimate raised the error to 2.5 mm, where the simulation had lowered it. Sphere2’s offset between the board’s point and the registered one, 1.4 mm, is 0.7 mm in another direction on this tip. Trained on 47 of cb1t’s own presses, the GP reached 0.71 mm and the MLP 0.42 mm (checkerboard fingertip, Sections 3, 6, 7 and 8). Corrected by a GP whose inputs are its own estimate, trained on the same presses, the physical model missed by 0.55 mm at 2 N and over. On turn holds at orientations that no press had it missed by 0.71 mm, where the GP on the board missed by 1.03 mm. Below 1 N the model and its correction both fail.

The tip v2 ID 1 has five N52 magnets, fitted at rest at 0.98 of an N52’s strength (UR5 sessions of 2026-10-26 and 27). Trained on its own 198 press actions, the GP places held-out contacts within 0.25 mm at 1.5 N and over and 0.66 mm below, as on tip 2. The physical model places presses under 1.5 N within 2.0 mm, where the v1 tips’ weaker magnets gave 8–10 mm (rows 20261027-v1_v2_tips.json). A GP of the v1 tips misses v2 ID 1’s contacts by 2.52 mm. It misses by 0.64 mm once each board change is scaled by its magnets’ strength (calibration on the UR5, Section 9). On the four checkerboard tips the own-press GP gives the force’s direction within 2.1–2.5° on the face at 1.5 N and over. On the edges it is within 3.1–4.6°, and on the flanks, where fewer presses were made, within 4.9–8.5° (rows 20261027-direction_by_region.json). A GP trained on v2 ID 1’s presses on the 12.5 mm rod places their contacts within 0.29 and 0.73 mm over and under 1.5 N. Its forces are within 0.22 N and 2.7° (rows rod_tips.json).

On the hand the other fingertips’ magnets add their field to each board. In v2 ID 1’s field model a five-magnet neighbour adds 513 µT with the pads facing and touching, and 4,162 µT side by side. A 0.5 N press changes the board by 23 µT. Subtracting the field predicted from a pose 0.3 mm and 0.3° off leaves 23 and 457 µT. When the neighbour’s pose is fitted from both boards, with the joint angles as a 1 mm, 1° prior, the bound on a press at the face’s centre is 0.147–0.149 N facing and 0.158–0.176 N side by side. With the pose known it is 0.147 N (magnetic crosstalk). The field of a second tip has not been measured.

The fingertip in the simulations

The simulations represent the tip by sphere pads, which are 0.75 mm spheres on a 1 mm lattice over its surface. Each pad has stiffness . In builder v2, the default since 2026-10-15, is the pad’s depth below the tip’s volume centroid. A stiff local modulus behind a series spring of 9.7 N/mm fits the FE model of the 11/22 tip within 5.6 % RMS in approach. With a spring in series, pads fitted to the FE pad follow the indentation measured on the UR5 within 135 µm RMS, against 133 µm for the FE pad. From the board’s force, the printed pad’s bulk is within about 22 % of the FE model. The estimator reports its forces at the same pads the simulations use, so a measured contact and a simulated one can be compared pad by pad. The fits, the turn they change in two simulators, the rod presses and the pads’ creep under the measured shear are in the contact overview (calibration of the pads).

Hardware built and measured

The DIP link holds the board against the pad. Three concepts were drawn: the window plate with a clamp (a), a cover that clamps the board behind the pad on rails (b) and a board printed over (c). On 2026-10-20 the owner chose b (“concept B is the clear winner”), which also resolves 0.028 against 0.065 N. In version 2 the board keeps its own Qwiic connector, and the cable lies in a groove past the slotted arm; both links are 9.75 mm longer (DIP link board mount). Version 3 adds 6 mm cover walls along the pad’s flanks, a column under the pad and a cable leg open to the top (DIP link b v3). Version 4 recesses the bridge’s palmar edge and shrinks the column. A flat object then meets the pad 4.0 mm before any rigid part, against 0.0 mm on v3. In a height test the owner chose 3 mm retaining walls. The snug covers 3S and 2S fit pad B05R at zero interference on the rails (DIP link b v4).

In the owner’s first presses by hand, on 2026-10-20, the pad rocked in its seat. After the fourth and fifth presses the reading stayed 62 and 104 µT from rest. A rigid shift of the whole pad by 17–23 µm, with a tilt of about 4 mrad, reproduces this. The estimator read the shift as standing contacts of 11–12 N. The same evening a cap went over the tip end, with a 2 mm pin into the pad (DIP link board mount). The viewer now adds a noise floor of 2 µT, shows a contact only above 0.25 N and takes a new baseline after 3 s at rest. No contact then shows at rest over a night (contact estimation, Section 9). On the UR5 the reference press kept its onset within 0.07 mm over 65 min.

The UR5 calibration mount clamps the DIP link to the HEX-E with the finger along the tool axis (UR5e mount v1). The pad’s normal force then falls on the sensor’s lateral axes. Version 3 takes the lab’s M6 × 20 screws, captive in the fork’s foot, with M3 heat-set inserts in the adapter; sphere2 ran on it with DIP link b v4 (mount v3). Pressed hard, the DIP link turns a little in the fork. Mount v4 adds a stop plate behind the link’s tongue with three set screws. Mount v5 replaces the screws by a PLA wedge, since the lab has no brass set screws. In the model either cuts the link’s turn under a face press from 1.0° to 0.05° (mount v4, mount v5). On 2026-10-23 the owner found v5’s wedge unusable, and cb1t ran on v3’s fork. Mount v6, a plate pressed onto the tongue’s back at four depths, waits on the owner’s choice.

Open questions

  1. The softness at a small contact. Under the sphere the presses travel 0.33 mm plus 0.20 mm/N beyond the FE pad’s indentation; under the rod, 0.07 mm plus 0.10 mm/N. At most 0.10 mm/N lies in series with the pad: in the DIP link’s clamp, the mount, the HEX-E, the arm or the indenter’s stand. At least 0.10 mm/N arises at the sphere’s contact, where the FE pad is stiffer than the print. The cause in the print has not been found.
  2. The registration along the finger. Sphere2’s own registration and a joint one with the rod’s and sph3t’s touch-offs fit them equally well. They place sphere2’s contacts a median 1.09 mm apart, 0.94 mm of it along the finger. Every touch-off met the indenter at its top, with a vertical contact normal, so none of them sees a horizontal shift of the indenter; that place rests on the homing seating. Twelve touch-offs aimed 3 mm beside the sphere’s top meet curved parts of the pad off the top. In the simulator, with the seating 0.6 mm off, they cut the contact error at the presses from 0.23 to 0.17 mm and from 1.36 to 0.04 mm under two sets of tool errors. On the checkerboard tip they moved the fitted sphere centre 1.96 mm and turned the pad’s frame 1.93°. With that registration the grid presses’ indentation beyond the FE pad fits within 108 µm RMS, against 142 µm before, and the board’s point lies 0.72 mm from the registered one, against 1.54 mm. Sphere2 and sph3t were registered with plain touch-offs only.
  3. Light presses. With the v1 magnets the untrained estimator places contacts below 1 N about 10 mm away. With five N52 magnets it places those under 1.5 N within 2.0 mm. The step of about 7 µT that each press leaves on the rest is the size of a 0.3 N press. Learned models give 1.1 to 2.5 mm there. On the checkerboard tip the estimator’s own position sigma flags most of these misses: 18 mm at 0.25 N, 3 mm at 1 N. A gate at 2 mm keeps 95–100 % of the holds at 2 N and over and 2–13 % below, where a few misses still pass.
  4. The force reference. The HEX-E’s Fz gain is 0.78–0.87 of its other axes’, and its link drops out; an ATI Mini45, once calibrated, is to replace it. The FE takes Siraya 85A at 12 MPa from a NinjaFlex datasheet. Through the board’s force, the UR5 session puts the printed pad within about 22 % of it.
  5. The magnets. The v1 tips’ magnets have 0.20–0.57 of an N52 magnet’s moment as fitted at rest, and v2 ID 1’s five N52 magnets 0.98. The models predict 0.028–0.031 N with N52, about 0.039 N at the measured noise. Four magnets (0.051 N) or five (0.029 N) waits on the owner. A touching neighbour that faces the pad adds 38 µT at the board with four magnets, against 513 µT with five.
  6. Transfer of learned models. The physical model transfers to a new pad through its rest calibration: on the checkerboard tip it placed contacts within 2.06 mm without a press. The GP correction learned on sphere2 does not, and raised that error to 2.48 mm. Fine-tuned with 20 of the new tip’s presses it gives 1.59 mm; the tip’s own 47 presses give 0.42–0.71 mm. Scaled by the magnets’ strength fitted at rest, the v1 tips’ presses place v2 ID 1’s contacts within 0.64 mm, against 2.52 mm unscaled.
  7. Disturbances in the hand. The other fingers’ magnets are modelled but not measured. Side by side and touching, a five-magnet neighbour adds 4,162 µT, and its pose must be fitted from the boards. Steel touched to the face reads as a press of 9 to 17.5 N. The test against fields from outside the pad removes most of those frames, but the first half second of a touch and fields of 40 to 90 µT still show 1 to 9 N. The chips’ temperature drift is measured, 0.65–0.70 % per °C, and the correction from each chip’s temperature leaves 9 of 70 µT over a warm-up. The magnets’ own coefficient, which follows the pad’s lagging temperature, is not separated yet.
  8. Large presses, shear and torsion. The FE is linear and frictionless; a neo-Hookean check lost 11 % of the force at 350 µm on the softest tip. The tip’s tangential compliance, 48–177 µm/N, is in neither simulator. On the checkerboard tip the estimator reports 1.08 N of shear where the HEX-E measures 0.25 N. A GP trained on the 3D force gets the shear within 0.12 N on held-out presses, but misses by 0.31 N at the turns’ new orientations. The twists’ torsion, half the difference between outbound and return, measures a median 2.9 N mm and up to 9.9 N mm at 2.5 N; a point torque in the physical model does not recover it from the board. On the UR5 the face’s normal lies across the tool axis. The torsion then lies under a push moment of about 230 N mm on the HEX-E (calibration protocol).
  9. The simulators. Calibrated to the FE, the pads and Drake agree on approach within 6 %. They end a turn 6.3° apart, with contact forces 0.37 N apart. Whether builder v2 stays the default waits on the owner.

Future work

  1. Compliance in series (QUEUE.md R16): put a dial indicator on the sphere’s block. Press a rigid part of the tool, the HEX-E’s adapter or the fork, on the sphere at 1 to 5 N. Travel of the block puts the compliance on the indenter’s side. Travel beyond the HEX-E’s data sheet with a still block puts it in the arm or the mount. Travel near the data sheet’s leaves the DIP link’s clamp for the series part, at most 0.10 mm/N.
  2. Softness at the sphere: press the FE pad’s printed twin with a 5 mm sphere on a bench under a dial indicator, the pad clamped on a rigid block, at 0.5 to 5 N. Travel near the sphere’s local part (UR5 results page, Section 8) confirms that the FE pad is too stiff under a sphere. Travel near the FE pad’s own places that part in the robot’s tool.
  3. Mount v6 (four squish depths, on the owner’s choice): print one, then repeat the rod’s touch-offs, registration and presses. A slope that stays at 0.10 mm/N under the rod rules out the link’s turn in the fork as the series part.
  4. Checkerboard tip’s poles: check each magnet’s pole at the palm face with a compass. The rest fit predicts north toward the palm at the bottom-left and top-right magnets, seen from the palm with the tip end up, and south at the other three. Any other result means wrong chip frames in the board’s calibration.
  5. ATI Mini45 (the ATI plan’s QUEUE.md, A1): run the box check, print the stack and run the 39 stations with the 100 g weight in its printed holder, or with 0.5 kg. Then repeat a grid of presses against the ATI. A board force outside 0.78–1.05 of the ATI’s means that the HEX-E’s gain biased sphere2’s comparison.
  6. Untrained estimator under the rod: score the viewer’s estimator on rod1’s 279 holds, as Table 3 of the UR5 results page scores it on sphere2’s. A location error well above the sphere’s 1.6–2.6 mm means that the estimator’s point-load basis misses line contacts.
  7. Second fingertip with known points and forces: clamp it in a printed jig with sphere seats at the reference point and 4 mm from it toward ±y and ±z. Press through a kitchen scale at about 1, 2 and 4 N. Run scripts/fingertip_second_tip_transfer.py --landmarks on the stretch. A GP correction whose median location error exceeds the physical model’s by more than 0.9 mm does not transfer across pole patterns.
  8. N52 magnets: recalibrate in the viewer (key c). A strength of 0.8–1.2, the poles as inserted and a rest residual below 0.43 mT confirm the field model. Then repeat the jig presses or a short UR5 grid; the simulation predicts 1.5 mm for the rebuilt physical model and 0.7 mm with the GP correction.
  9. Torsion on the HEX-E’s axis: twist the pad at 5 N on a fixture that puts the face’s normal along the tool axis. The torsion is half the difference between the outbound and return holds. A torque outside the sphere pads’ friction torque at the measured friction coefficient falsifies the pads’ torsion.
  10. Sensing rows on the probes’ gap rule: run_sense in scripts/v2_tip_fe_checks.py takes its gaps from tpu_tip_magnet.gaps. That function moves a face node onto the analytic surface only within half a grid cell of it. It gives 150 µm against the probe rows’ 185 for the same pad at 1 N. Rerun --sense b_v2 with every face node on the surface; a force resolution that moves by more than 5 % means the DIP page’s resolutions need the same rerun.
  11. Facing finger: record the board with a second tip’s magnets at 20–40 mm and compare with the dipole prediction before subtracting it from the joint angles.
  12. Steel at known distances and forces: touch the 100 g mass and the ruler through printed spacers of 0.5 to 10 mm, then set the mass on the face (0.98 N). Run scripts/fingertip_foreign_field.py touches on each stretch. A spacer reading over 100 µT with Λ under 25 means the test misses steel. A joint fit of a contact and the far field within 0.3 N of 0.98 N would measure presses made with steel.
  13. Temperature: with the pad at rest and the viewer logging, hold a warm hand around the finger for 60 s and take it away. Run scripts/fingertip_contact_estimation_study.py thermal on that stretch. No contact should show while the chips warm by 2–3 °C. A drift that grows with the temperature after the correction means the magnets need a coefficient of their own. Firmware with TCMP_EN 1 is the alternative, to be tested the same way.
  14. Fingertips beside each other on the hand (owner, 2026-10-25): once every fingertip has its UR5 calibration, mount them on the SR2 hand. Record the boards through a wide range of finger motions, with the joint angles. Fit each fingertip’s field at its neighbours’ chips as a function of those angles. Laid against each other on the desk, three fingertips moved each other’s rest by 210 to 991 µT. With the re-zero, no contact was shown at rest in 39 minutes (src/morphohand/driver/reskin5x/README.md). The fitted model fails if, during motion, it leaves a contact shown on a fingertip that nothing touches.
